description_full: First Financial Corporation operates as the bank holding company for First Financial Bank N.A. that provides various financial services for individuals and businesses in west-central Indiana, east-central Illinois, western Kentucky, central and eastern Tennessee, and northern Georgia in the United States. The company offers non-interest-bearing demand, interest-bearing demand, savings, time, and other time deposits; checking and savings accounts; personal and business certificates of deposit; and digital banking services. It also provides commercial loans primarily to expand a business or finance asset purchases; real estate mortgages, including residential real estate and residential real estate construction loans; home equity loans and lines, secured loans, cash/CD secured loans, and unsecured loans; mortgage refinance; personal and auto loans; and credit cards. In addition, the company offers lease financing, trust account, and depositor services; business services, including accounts receivable and payable, merchant services, fraud protection, money management, and workplace rewards; and wealth services. The company was formerly known as Terre Haute First Corporation and changed its name to First Financial Corporation in December 1984. First Financial Corporation was founded in 1834 and is headquartered in Terre Haute, Indiana.

financial_summary: First Financial Corporation is a small-cap financial services business with a $918M market cap on $262M of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +12% over the past three years and +6% annually across the full decade, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder.
Returns on capital run at 9% against a 9% cost of capital, which means the business barely earns its keep economically.

The business throws off $86M in free cash flow — roughly 33 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.14× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 1.7× net debt/EBITDA, and thin 1.1× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.
Shareholder yield of 2.7% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 5.0% of the shares.

sector_headwinds.text: Altman Z in the distress zone (0.4) — the kind of balance-sheet risk that can make a loss permanent
Low reinvestment-driven growth suggests the compounding engine has stalled
Credit cycles and regulatory capital — losses accumulate invisibly in good years and appear all at once, and the time to worry is when underwriting standards are loosest.
Fintech disintermediation — neobanks, embedded finance, and blockchain rails are unbundling the fee streams that traditional banks took for granted.
Interest rate regime shifts — a rapid move in rates can invert the yield curve, crush bond portfolios, and trigger deposit flight simultaneously.
